# 1.2.46 - the sidebar's own strip, and a year of red that was not red

A fix for something 1.2.45 broke, and then the consequences of looking
properly at what the tests had been saying. No rule changed. The copy is still
the copy - its rewording comes with 1.3.0.

**The stack keeps off the sidebar.** On anything narrower than a desk the
module's blocks stack in one column at the top of the screen, and in 1.2.45 that
column ran to eight pixels off the right wall. Foundry's sidebar tab rail stands
in the last fifty or so, and it is painted after the stack: measured at every
stacked size, forty-eight pixels of every row were behind it - which on the
Despair rail is exactly where the counts are and on the status strip exactly
where Hope is. The stack now measures that rail and stops short of it.

The same measurement found a second one. The notice tile sits at the foot of the
screen, and the scene controls - pushed down to make room for the stack - end up
where the cards are. Nothing had become unreachable, because the notices take no
clicks, but a card was standing on the tool rail. Both of the tile's edges are
measured now.

Holding the sidebar's width back cost the Despair row fifty-six pixels and sent
the stepper to a line of its own again. The row does not wrap at all now, which
is what lets it fit: a wrapping row places its parts on lines before any of them
may shrink, so the run of pips never gave up a pixel. Held to one line, the pips
are the only part that can give, and twelve of them read as well in two rows of
six.

**Things a screen reader can now read.** Every control in the module is a real
button - that part was right from the start - but a good few of them were an
icon and a tooltip, and a tooltip is drawn, not announced. They carry a name
now, taken from what each one already had. The notice stack and the Event card
are polite live regions, so a card that arrives on its own is read out instead of
appearing in silence, and focus moves into a module window when it opens.

In Windows' high-contrast modes - anything that sets `forced-colors` - the
curtain and the dressed window bands step aside. They are painted into canvases,
which a forced palette cannot reach inside, so they would have sat on top of the
system's own background as a dark picture. Everything else is a box with words
in it, which forced colours can draw: a system border, the system's two colours,
and the blur and glow off so they cannot muddy what is left. A Despair pip says
"spent" with a colour and an opacity and both are taken there, so it says it with
an outline instead. `prefers-contrast: more` takes the theme's one deliberately
dimmed colour up to full strength. The prep badge is a shade deeper, which is the
one place in the theme where the GM's red carried words and did not quite have
the contrast for them.

**Two new commands, for questions that could not be answered from here.**
`game.drpg.perf()` reports what the theme costs the machine it is running on:
the frame budget as it stands, the frame budget with the curtain's pulse held
off, the difference between them, one recut of the glass and the module's own
hot lookups. Every performance number this project had was measured headlessly,
where a canvas is composited in software, and none of them said anything
trustworthy about a real machine. `game.drpg.a11y()` lists any control in the
module's chrome that still has no name to be read out.

**And the part with no visible effect at all.** Twelve of the module's own tests
failed on every headless run, under a label that said they needed a real browser.
Four of them did not. Three were the test harness reading a document's fields
under the wrong name - which is why a test about diagonal walls had been
reporting a fault in code that was correct all along - one used a DOM property
that only browsers have, and one was refused by an inventory cap that the tests
before it had filled. All five run now. The nine that remain really do need a
browser and each says which part of one, and the runner counts them apart from
failures, so a genuine fault stands out the moment it appears instead of joining
a number people had learnt to read past.

**For the table.** If anything behaves differently after this update other than
on a narrow screen, that is a bug, and the version to compare against is 1.2.45.
